clue.text: Weekly issue with attractive features

parts.note: an issue is a child, and 'weekly' points to a day of the week; the nursery rhyme says the child born on that day is fair of face

explanation.walkthrough: 'Weekly issue' looks like a magazine. The rhyme runs 'Monday's child is fair of face', so the child of the first weekday has the attractive features.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old nursery rhyme the infant born on the first weekday is fair of face, which matches offspring with good looks.

clue.text: Master composer and nothing more ?

indicators.note: a composer puts things together, so here the letters of the first word are put into a new order

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A great composer is described as no more than that.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange MASTER to MAESTR and add O for 'nothing'; the whole clue also describes a great musician.
explanation.definitionFit: An eminent conductor or composer is addressed with this Italian title for a master.

clue.text: Nijinsky was heard to refuse ?

parts.note: Nijinsky was a famous racehorse, and a horse's call sounds like saying 'nay', a refusal

explanation.walkthrough: Nijinsky seems to be the ballet dancer, but here it is the racehorse that won the Triple Crown in 1970; a horse's cry sounds like the past of 'nay', to refuse.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse such as Nijinsky makes its high whinny, and that sound resembles a refusal.

clue.text: South American native like Long John ?

explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the country around Buenos Aires is one; the adjective also means silvery, and Long John is the pirate surnamed Silver.

clue.text: Myrtle, for instance, gets drunk

explanation.definitionFit: Myrtle is a woody bush; the word also names an old cordial of fruit juice and rum, something taken as a drink.

clue.text: Tonsorial nightmare for Damocles

parts.note: Damocles sat beneath a sword hanging by a single hair, so a barber snipping that hair would be his dread

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tonsorial' means to do with barbers; Damocles sat beneath a sword hung by one hair, so his worst visit to the barber would sever it.
explanation.definitionFit: A visit to the barber snips hairs, and one snipped hair would drop the sword on Damocles.

clue.text: There's nothing liable to change in the garden

definitions.text: There's nothing liable to change in the garden

indicators.note: to change asks that the letters of the word liable, with the zero, be rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that nothing in the beds ever seems to alter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To change' rearranges O (for 'nothing') and LIABLE into a garden flower.
explanation.definitionFit: This blue-flowered bedding plant is a garden favourite.

clue.text: Lullaby of the downfall of a swinging chick?

definitions.text: the downfall of a swinging chick

explanation.definitionFit: The nursery song is sung to settle infants, and it ends with the cradle swinging in the treetop falling, baby and all.

clue.text: Opportunity for a night at the theatre

definitions.text: for a night at the theatre

explanation.definitionFit: A chance or gap is an opportunity; the first night of a play is its premiere, so the word also qualifies that night.

clue.text: Heavenly display by Apollo and Jupiter Pluvius

parts.note: Jupiter Pluvius is the Roman god in his role as sender of showers, so he stands for rain
Apollo is the archer god, whose emblem is the bow

explanation.surface: Two classical gods put on a show across the sky together.
explanation.walkthrough: The gods are not named for their letters but for their attributes: the archer god gives his weapon, the god of showers gives what he sends.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc of colours across the sky after a shower is a celestial spectacle.

clue.text: Saving of reputations as shown in TV commercials

explanation.definitionFit: Covering up faults restores a good name; washing-powder adverts show laundry made brighter.

clue.text: A man's inside, the nick's reformed to cope

indicators.note: reformed means made over into a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the words 'the nick' give their seven letters as fodder; the possessive adds none

explanation.surface: An inmate is inside the prison, and has reformed in order to get by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' and 'the nick' (British slang for prison) suggest a man serving time. The seven letters of THE NICK, reformed, spell the room where food is prepared, here the old slang for a man's stomach; 'to cope' is a loose link.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang treats the stomach as the body's cookhouse, where food is dealt with.

clue.text: Bill, self-contained, one gets for bacteria

indicators.note: self-contained here means the bill holds a bill of its own inside it

parts.note: taken as the name itself
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A man called Bill lives in a self-contained flat and picks up a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-contained' is the trick: the name Bill holds another word for a bill (an account) inside itself, rather than describing a flat.
explanation.definitionFit: These rod-shaped microbes are a common class of germ.

clue.text: Central heating system in the red ?

definitions.text: Central heating system in the red ?

parts.words: Central heating system in the red ?
parts.note: the body's warmth is carried round from the heart by a red fluid, so the domestic heating phrase describes it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Central heating' and 'in the red' sound like household bills and debt; the circulation is the body's heating, and it is red.
explanation.definitionFit: The red fluid pumped by the heart carries warmth round the body like water through radiators.

clue.text: Aunt and I involved with fate turn to folly

indicators.note: involved means tangled up together, so the letters of the words around it are mixed

explanation.surface: An aunt and her relative get mixed up with destiny and act foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involved' scrambles AUNT, I and FATE together.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone besotted is an old sense of driving them to foolishness.

clue.text: Organizing a feast isn't characteristic of Billy Bunter

indicators.note: organizing puts things into a new order, so the letters following are rearranged

explanation.surface: Laying on a banquet is not something the greedy schoolboy would do.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the greedy, plump schoolboy of Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories. 'Organizing' rearranges FEAST and ISNT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greyfriars schoolboy is famous for his greed and his girth, so plumpness is his trait.

clue.text: Agitated like the bull that is in the net perhaps

indicators.note: in places the bull and the abbreviation inside the rearranged letters
perhaps hints that the word net is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: taken as the animal's own name
that is translates the Latin id est, abbreviated IE

explanation.surface: A bull caught in a net is understandably worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that the net is one arrangement of its letters, giving ENT, and 'in' places the animal and 'that is' within it; 'like the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubbling over with high spirits is a state of excitement.

clue.text: In difficulties like Charles -II?

explanation.definitionFit: Being stuck in a fix is an idiom; Charles the Second hid in an oak at Boscobel after the battle of Worcester.

clue.text: Explosive townsman in Kent

explanation.definitionFit: This picric-acid high explosive was named after the Kentish town of Lydd, where it was tested, and a resident of that town would be called the same.

clue.text: He plotted both ends of that Burning Deck affair

indicators.note: both ends of says only the start and finish of that title are kept, the middle dropped

parts.note: Casabianca is the poem beginning 'The boy stood on the burning deck'

explanation.surface: A conspirator was behind a famous shipboard disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem 'Casabianca' was a schoolroom staple; keep its first three and last two letters. The definition is one of the Roman conspirators against Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: This senator was one of the conspirators who planned and struck the first blow against Julius Caesar.

clue.text: Capital measure upset

parts.note: a capital letter is called a cap
size is a measure of how big something is

explanation.surface: A city's dimensions are thrown into turmoil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like a city but gives CAP, a printer's word for a capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To overturn a boat is to tip it over.

clue.text: No motion study, this

parts.note: the branch of mechanics dealing with bodies at rest studies forces without movement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Motion study' sounds like time-and-motion work; the branch of mechanics concerned with bodies at rest studies no motion.
explanation.definitionFit: The part of mechanics treating forces in equilibrium deals with stationary bodies.

clue.text: Caveman of fantastic polish

parts.note: the hero of the Arabian Nights tale enters a cave of treasure and summons a genie by rubbing a lamp

explanation.walkthrough: 'Caveman' suggests a prehistoric man; this one went into a magic cave, and his polishing of the lamp was fantastic in the fairy-tale sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian Nights hero goes into an enchanted cave and conjures a genie by rubbing a lamp.

clue.text: Punch a King!

explanation.definitionFit: A hot spiced wine drink is a kind of toddy; it is also the Ethiopian title for a monarch.

clue.text: Call to account the self-. identification of beauty

parts.note: saying who you are begins 'I am', shortened to I'M
a peach is an old word for a lovely person

explanation.surface: A beauty is made to answer for her vanity in introducing herself.
explanation.walkthrough: A beauty introducing herself would say 'I'm a peach', which runs together as the word for charging an official.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge a public official with misconduct is to make them answer for it.

clue.text: Treating to a high-ball? Not on this outing

definitions.text: Treating to a high-ball? Not on this outing

parts.words: Treating to a high-ball? Not on this outing
parts.note: in cricket a bowler can deliver a full ball aimed at the batsman's feet, the opposite of a high ball

explanation.walkthrough: 'Treating to a high-ball' sounds like buying a drink. In cricket a yorker is a ball pitched at the batsman's feet, so getting a batsman out with one is anything but a high ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowling a batsman with a delivery pitched right at the feet is a cricket term derived from the low full ball.

clue.text: Noted ones forming an impression

indicators.note: forming means shaping into something, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: two ones written as Roman numerals are II

explanation.surface: Respected people help create a good impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ones' gives two Roman ones, II, and 'forming' rearranges them with NOTED.
explanation.definitionFit: A print run of a book is called an impression or issue.

clue.text: Number of relatively near misses on the London road

explanation.definitionFit: Siblings who are female are close relatives and unmarried girls, seven of them a number; Seven Sisters Road runs through north London.
